hook: If you've tried journalling, breathing, and positive affirmations — and you still can't stop the thoughts — you're not doing it wrong. You're using the right tools on the wrong problem.
topic: Why common interventions fail and what category of problem intrusive thoughts actually are
body:
**Breathing exercises work on your nervous system. Journalling works on your narrative. Affirmations work on your beliefs.**

None of them work on the mechanism that's actually running.

Negative thought loops aren't a belief problem. They're not a breathing problem. They're a pattern-completion problem. Your brain has a well-worn neural pathway — a thought arises, you react to it, you try to suppress it, it rebounds louder, you react more. That's the loop. Every time you engage with it — even to fight it — you deepen the track.

What interrupts that loop isn't force. It's non-engagement.

The technique that has the most clinical support for this is called cognitive defusion. You don't argue with the thought. You don't replace it. You just change your relationship to it. You observe it. You name it. "There's a thought telling me I'm going to fail." Not "I'm going to fail." There's a thought telling me.

That one grammatical shift creates separation. And separation breaks the loop.

I have a full guide on this process — link in my bio.
